title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary English as a foreign language (EFL) students engineered prompts while using ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a writing task. The main problem addressed is that although generative AI may support EFL writing, non-technical students often do not know how to prompt these systems effectively and instead proceed through trial and error. The study asks what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns characterize their prompt engineering pathways during a writing activity.

The researchers conducted a qualitative multiple-case study focused on students’ turns of interaction with chatbots during a timed blog-writing task. Four students completed the same writing task using an iPad, Google Docs, and the POE app, which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly. Data came primarily from screen recordings of students’ interactions and were supplemented by the completed writing products. The analysis used content coding of prompts and visualization of prompt sequences to identify types of prompt content and pathway patterns.

The population consisted of four Form One students in a Hong Kong secondary school who were high-achieving in English and had some prior experience with other generative AI tools, but were using these chatbots for writing for the first time. The activity took place in a classroom during an after-school lesson and lasted up to 45 minutes. Students received no explicit instruction on chatbot capabilities or prompt engineering before beginning the task.

The study concludes that students followed distinct prompt engineering pathways, using different combinations and sequences of prompt types such as auto-complete prompts, natural language instructions, questions, search-style prompts, and chatbot-suggested prompts. Some pathways appeared more sophisticated than others, especially when students combined prompt types or iteratively refined prompts. The authors argue that EFL students need explicit prompt engineering education to move beyond individual trial-and-error use and to better leverage chatbot capabilities in writing classrooms.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative multiple-case study with clear methods, direct K-12 relevance, and systematic coding, but no causal design, control group, or validated outcome measures. It therefore provides exploratory evidence with limited credibility for effectiveness claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially useful development of prompt-engineering skills in a priority K-12 EFL context, but impact on literacy outcomes is unclear and not quantified. No effect sizes or externally measured learning gains are reported.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots (via the Poe app) to help complete a timed English blog-writing task, with the study focusing on students' prompt engineering pathways during human-AI collaborative writing.
Students interacted conversationally with ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly as generative chatbots to elicit ideas and text continuations while composing an EFL writing task.

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines how four Hong Kong secondary EFL students (n=4) prompted ChatGPT and similar chatbots while completing a blog-writing task, identifying six prompt-content types and four distinct prompt-engineering pathways. Although the authors suggest some pathways appeared more sophisticated and discuss implications for supporting writing, the study does not directly measure writing-quality improvement, revision gains, or literacy achievement with validated external assessments or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Qualitative content analysis of prompts and completed writing products; number, type, and sequence of prompts during an EFL writing task

finding.finding_summary: Across 36 analyzed turns from 4 secondary EFL students, the study found students engaged in trial-and-error prompt engineering, with some students progressing from simpler prompt forms (e.g., auto-complete) to more complex combinations (e.g., natural language instruction plus exemplars and questions). The authors interpret this as evidence of emerging prompt-engineering skill and AI literacy development, though no standardized durable-skills measure or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Observed prompt-engineering behaviors, sophistication of prompt types, and pathway patterns from screen recordings
